searchText: <@!784446040073175040> and I would like to thank everyone for their time on the eth2 call. The PR (https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/pull/2454) has seen some healthy debate around the proposed 0x02 withdrawal credential solution. Please continue to contribute to the discussion - having multiple perspectives can only strengthen the ultimate solution. To reiterate the problem we have encountered: decentralised staking pools (such as Rocket Pool) that promote independent node operators are unfairly disadvantaged compared to centralised pools (which control their own nodes). As isidorosp said in the PR comments: "the concern around network/ecosystem health from any possible increased incentives for side-channeling payments for block production should be weighed against the concern of a non-decentralized staking landscape, and the latter is more important, especially when considering the ethos of Ethereum in general." For evidence on why this latter point is compelling: https://twitter.com/sparkpool_eth/status/1395662646951641090 We feel this is an important issue to be addressed for a variety of reasons, but we are supportive of the eth2 implementors' efforts to minimise scope creep to ensure delivery. *If* the solution was refined and agreed we would not require it to be part of the merge. Similar to 0x01 we would be fine with a promise. We would assume that when withdrawals are implemented (approx next hard fork after merge) it would be an opportune time for 0x02 to be implemented. Many thanks again and we look forward to discussing the proposal further. <@!301186049323958275> <@!425572898787426305> <@!291925846556540928> <@!755590043632140352> <@!219015859182632960> <@!273808422753796097> I am of the opinion that the thing we want to strongly encourage as much as possible is that each validator operates their own execution client and consensus client. I think that ensuring that solo staking has the most "advantages" over both decentralized and centralized pools is the most important endpoint to target. In fact, I am of the opinion (not shared by all) that if we can do things to actively make pooling unattractive we *should* because pooling in general is bad for the long-term health of the platform. While I agree that decentralized staking pools are better than centralized staking pools, any change that makes *any* pool better than or equal to solo validators is a bit of a non-starter. (this is separate from the arguments I made in the EIP, though it does give insight into my biases) solo staking > decentralized pool staking > centralized pool staking This change would remove one of the advantages of solo staking over decentralized staking, which would both make decentralized pool staking even better than centralized pool staking, but it would *also* reduce the benefit of solo staking over decentralized staking. I don't mean to be disrespectful, but I mean... it costs $84,000 USD to solo stake right now The goal of staking isn't to turn everyone into stakers or provide a social good. It is to secure the network. > This change would remove one of the advantages of solo staking over decentralized staking What advantage are you referring to here? The way to achieve this is to have as many unique/independent actors involved in the staking process as possible. Understood but pools do exist and currently centralised pools have the advantage. A centralized pool gets a lot of people involved, but there is only one decision making actor. A decentralized pool is better, the involved people have weak decision making power, but it is still fairly limited compared to solo stakers. This is exactly what a decentralised pool does. Reducing trust requirements. Currently, solo staking has 0 external trust requirements. The proposed change would *reduce* the trust requirements of decentralized staking, thus making it more attractive from a trust minimization standpoint and thus giving solo staking less of an edge over decentralized pool staking. Can someone remind me, how many blocks to finality in PoS? In our model, each validator is an individual node operator - running their own consensus and execution client. Decentralized staking pools definitely get people *more* involved than centralized staking pools, I agree. Well to be fair, they can use Infura or Pocket for ETH1 But yes That's the same story with solo staking today Yeah, the Infura/Pocket problem is separate I think and we can ignore it for this discussion. 🙂 Sure How does rocket pool decide what to vote on? In terms of block proposals? For voting in general with the 32 ETH validator. (including block proposals) The infrastructure is identical to solo staking, the only difference is a validator is comprised of 16 ETH from the node operator, and 16 from the staking pool When it's time to withdraw, the total validator balance is sent to a smart contract that disberses the appropriate amounts to each party appropriately I guess, but that isn't a big driver for many people unfortunately. I personally would prefer stronger _financial_ incentives (which mostly favor large centralized pools at the moment). But otherwise, Rocket Pool node operators are identical to solo stakers So the person running the consensus client and execution client have 16 ETH stake, and then there is 16 ETH stake from random people on the internet who tag along essentially? Correct While I agree 100% that we should be trying to benefit single stakers over any form of pool, and this can be seen in my passionately fighting over small things like bad head votes on late blocks or the later 3% rewards on the sync committee. There are larger effects that as far as I'm being told are unavoidable. So if things like MEV is a thing that can't be avoided. Then I'd argue that solo staking is just for the altruistic person that wants to help the network. Thinking on the interests of that solo staker: he is currently presented with two options, either forfeit MEV earnings that may be a relevant part of rewards, or move to a centralized pool. I'm afraid that the lack of this solution or a similar one will cause solo stakers to move to a centralized pool instead of a decentralized one which is the lesser of two evils. But the node operators stake is at risk first. In other words they take the hit on any penalties. The reason I think solo pools are healthier for the network than decentralized pools like this (and all other designs I have seen proposed) is that it gives leverage to an attacker. Essentially, an attacker now needs half as much money to attack the network because they can double their "voting power" by being a rocket pool node operator. This is most impactful for attacks where you *expect* to lose 100% of your stake as part of the attack but make it back in some other way. You now need half as much ETH to execute such an attack, which halves the security of the network against such classes of attacks. It's not exactly half, because they need to include some supplemental insurance to counter that kind of attack, but such an attack is still prohibitively expensive to launch Today, yes. Tomorrow, 🤷 That 1.6+ ETH worth of RPL is not much of a supplemental insurance imo Ok We should be designing these systems so they work at all scales and don't depend on any particular valuation of anything. But we haven't. We strive to (usually). We don't always succeed, but we try to get as close as possible. Ideally the vast majority of validators would be solo validators and they would be incentivized via the protocol as such, but they aren't. It's unfortunate and it's probably also very difficult (if not impossible) to do properly I agree, and I *think* many others would agree that such a goal is ideal. Because you'd need some kind of built in sybil resistance But we need not let the perfect be the enemy of the good. Which leaves us with the question, which is worse: More solo validators, but also more centralized pool validators, or fewer solo validators and fewer centralized pool validators? So the reality is that you have centralized/quasi-decentralized (i.e. permissioned) staking pools who will leverage economies of scale and take on the balance of stake ETH concentration I would say the same thing about `coinbase` versus side-channel problems FWIW, it is not *obviously* clear that weakening decentralized validators is the optimal solution. I believe it is in this case, but I can definitely appreciate that not everyone will agree on this. I'm not sure that dichotomy is completely fair, but honestly I would go for the latter Unless I misunderstood, this is not how things will play out in reality though - the pie chart <@!376562530463776787> linked makes that quite clear There is a large market for people that want to stake but cannot afford a solo validator, and they are going to stake one way or another That is, if you decrease the distance between solo and decentralized pools, while at the same time increasing the distance between decentralized pools and centralized pools, that may be a worthy trade. You'll lose solo validators to decentralized pool validators, and you'll also lose centralized validators to decentralized pool validators. I mean it's *already* clear that centralized staking services have a huge foothold and are growing faster than anything else... so what do we do? if decentralized pools cannot compete, small stakers will go to centralized exchanges, since they cannot become solo stakers That is our mission indeed I think this is a very reasonable argument, even if I disagree at the moment. Do note that liquidity also comes into play here. Even without decentralized pools, one could still think of a way of allowing solo stakers to use their staked balance as collateral (with the other party assuming a certain counterparty risk of course) Out of curiosity, how much ETH is currently staked by people who have less than 32 ETH? How much by people with more than 32 ETH? The day we come up with a mechanism to let people run solo validators in such a way that pools are obsolete is the day I retire Until then, we fight the good fight haha Currently 64 under optimal conditions. I'm not sure why the question though I don't think we can know to be honest Do tell People with >32 ETH can choose not to solo validate (i.e. validate via a centralized staking service, or LIDO, or whatnot) I wanted to validate my assumptions about the human response time necessary for defending against a noticed validator attack. ~12 minutes means we cannot rely on social consensus to stop an attack against finality, and we cannot reasonably roll back finality with consensus changes. True, just because you have the capital doesn't mean you want to (or know how to) manage a node Well one of the most efficient forms of capital allocation is to allow experts to do it for you 🙂 Well, it's basically all the RocketPool stuff, but requiring 32 ETH for a validator instead of 16 + 16, no? It'd still be locked up though I must have misunderstood your liquidity comment All forms of "follow the leader/expert" staking lead to the "attack cost reduction" problem. If there is a valid attack it will take longer than two epochs to finalize (unless the attacker has a vast majority of the network) No, I think you got me, I just didn't think it through 😅 We want as many unique actors *making human decisions* as possible, that is what gets us security. <@!784446040073175040> and I would like to thank everyone for their time on the eth2 call.

The PR (https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/pull/2454) has seen some healthy debate around the proposed 0x02 withdrawal credential solution. Please continue to contribute to the discussion - having multiple perspectives can only strengthen the ultimate solution.

To reiterate the problem we have encountered: decentralised staking pools (such as Rocket Pool) that promote independent node operators are unfairly disadvantaged compared to centralised pools (which control their own nodes).
As isidorosp said in the PR comments:
"the concern around network/ecosystem health from any possible increased incentives for side-channeling payments for block production should be weighed against the concern of a non-decentralized staking landscape, and the latter is more important, especially when considering the ethos of Ethereum in general."

For evidence on why this latter point is compelling: 
https://twitter.com/sparkpool_eth/status/1395662646951641090

We feel this is an important issue to be addressed for a variety of reasons, but we are supportive of the eth2 implementors' efforts to minimise scope creep to ensure delivery. *If* the solution was refined and agreed we would not require it to be part of the merge. Similar to 0x01 we would be fine with a promise. We would assume that when withdrawals are implemented (approx next hard fork after merge) it would be an opportune time for 0x02 to be implemented.

Many thanks again and we look forward to discussing the proposal further.
